The last turbine is currently operating safely,” Magyar said on social media. The plant already operates at a reduced capacity of just over 10% after the Danube fell to a record low, making it impossible to cool it properly. Energy minister István Kapitány said on Tuesday that a number of energy saving measures succeeded in lowering energy consumption to keep the grid secure. https://www.planetf1.com/news/fia-max-ve.text: Max Verstappen has had a few skirmishes with the FIA over the course of his F1 career The FIA has confirmed that Red Bull driver Max Verstappen will face no further action after an incident with Williams’ Carlos Sainz in practice at the Hungarian Grand Prix. Verstappen was summoned to the stewards on Friday following an incident with Sainz in the early stages of FP1. Max Verstappen escapes FIA action after Carlos Sainz investigation Want more PlanetF1.com coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google for news you can trust Verstappen encountered a slow-moving Sainz on the approach to Turn 12, forcing the Red Bull driver to abandon a lap. He then appeared to retaliate by deliberately slowing on the exit of the corner to the Turn 13 hairpin, obstructing Sainz and the Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto. Verstappen found himself under investigation for erratic driving, requiring the four-time world champion to visit the stewards after FP1. Max Verstappen vs Isack Hadjar: Red Bull head-to-head stats for F1 2026 season F1 2026: Head-to-head qualifying records between teammates F1 2026: Head-to-head race statistics between teammates With Sainz insisting that he was ‘not in any way affected’ by Verstappen slowing down on the exit of Turn 12, however, the stewards opted against taking further action. The stewards’ report read: “The Stewards heard from the drivers of Car 3 (Max Verstappen) and Car 55 (Carlos Sainz) and the team representatives and reviewed video, telemetry, team radio and in-car video evidence. “On the approach to turn 12, Car 3 had to move off the racing line to avoid Car 55 which had slowed unexpectedly on the racing line. “The Driver of Car 3 then slowed significantly at turn 12 and gesticulated to the driver of Car 55 to mark his frustration that he had been impeded by Car 55. “The driver of Car 55 then overtook Car 3. “The driver of Car 55 said that he was not in any way affected by Car 3 slowing at turn 12. No other car was affected. “The Stewards therefore determined to take no further action.” As reported by PlanetF1.com , Sainz was given a warning for his role in the incident despite drawing attention to an issue with his team radio communications at the time. Verstappen remains without a victory in the F1 2026 season entering the Hungarian Grand Prix weekend. The 28-year-old has been limited to just three podium finishes this year, recording a best result of second place at Red Bull’s home race in Austria. Verstappen also finished third in Canada and Belgium. Although he is officially under contract until the end of the 2028 season, it is widely believed that a clause in his contract will allow him to leave Red Bull if he is lower than second in the drivers’ standings at the summer break. Verstappen currently sits seventh, trailing second-placed Lewis Hamilton by 68 points with just 25 available in Hungary, the final race before the August shutdown. PlanetF1.com revealed last month that Verstappen is in advanced talks with McLaren over a move for 2027. However, it is unclear if he will commit to leaving his current team. Parker was killed, police said, when her car collided with a pickup truck driven by 63-year-old George Cole of Akron, Ohio. Investigators said Parker was driving a 2026 Toyota Camry northbound on Route 11 when it crossed into the southbound lane, hitting the 2019 Ram pickup truck towing a camper. Parker was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the sheriff’s office. A passenger in the Toyota, Tony Parker, sustained apparent minor injuries and was transported to Central Maine Medical Center by Poland Fire and Rescue, authorities said. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-leade.text: DUBLIN — EU leaders gathering in Dublin on Friday will continue arguing over who should represent them in talks about Ukraine’s future after a day of ferocious diplomatic activity. As Donald Trump’s administration intensifies its efforts to broker an end to Russia’s war and Europe may have secured a place at the table, bickering over who will speak on behalf of the bloc already looks like overshadowing the summit in the Irish capital — that wasn’t even supposed to be about Ukraine in the first place. “You could even have a TV show about it,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal joked to POLITICO in an interview on Thursday, in a sign of just how stark the divisions have become among leaders. “But we are saving the best part for tomorrow.” Advertisement Advertisement Russia’s full-scale invasion started in February 2022 and as Trump’s enthusiasm for brokering peace has ebbed and flowed, the EU has found itself edged out of the picture ― despite increasingly picking up the tab . Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who met with about 50 EU and non-EU leaders in Dublin on Thursday, warned that Russia was seeking to reshape Europe’s security architecture and insisted that European governments must have a voice in the negotiations, following two days of Russia-Ukraine-U.S. negotiations in Abu Dhabi that largely left out the EU. Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, discussed the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier on Thursday before the American pair touched down in Dublin in the evening to offer Zelenskyy their thoughts. The EU is united over the need to have a seat at the table as Ukraine’s main backer, but not on who it should send, with diplomats and officials telling POLITICO that the bloc has split into at least three camps. In one, there is growing support for European Council President António Costa, whose role makes him the natural candidate to represent the bloc. In another, there’s France and Germany, both of which are reluctant to surrender their own places at the negotiating table to Brussels. And then there’s the loneliest camp of all, the backers of Kaja Kallas. The bloc’s top diplomat would be the obvious pick, if not for her hawkishness on Russia, which some diplomats say could put off the Kremlin and make her a liability. Advertisement Advertisement Costa is accountable When it comes to speaking for Europe, there’s one man who’s already got that in his job description. Costa is emerging as the most broadly acceptable candidate among EU capitals. His institutional role gives him a mandate to represent the bloc’s leaders on the world stage, while his position and background as a former Portuguese prime minister afford him some neutrality, according to a European diplomat, who was granted anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the discussions. Estonia’s Michal was the first leader to come out in support of Costa, telling POLITICO his “mandate comes directly from the [European] Council” and makes him “accountable” to the EU’s member countries. Costa arrives at the ninth meeting of the European Political Community (EPC), in Dublin on November 12, 2026 | Paul Faith / AFP via Getty Images Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who called for the issue to be added to the agenda of Friday’s talks, said she would be OK with Costa, while Luxembourg and Poland’s leaders also backed him in remarks to reporters Thursday. Costa himself has also made it clear that the EU is represented internationally by its institutions — meaning him. Kallas, however, is a much more divisive proposition. Advertisement Advertisement Some diplomats see the former Estonian prime minister, who an EU official once said eats “Russians for “breakfast,” as an unacceptable interlocutor for the Kremlin. “That’s a joke, right?” another European diplomat said of the prospect of Kallas representing the EU in the high-stakes talks, describing her as “probably the worst person you could pick.” But others argue that it’s precisely this hawkish reputation that makes her the right person for the job. “It would make much more sense,” a second senior European diplomat told POLITICO. “That’s what Putin would do. He would pick whoever you don’t want to talk to.” Michal argued Kallas’ role makes her a natural second to Costa, and that both will presumably be in their positions until their terms end in 2029, making them more reliable than a national leader. “Putin doesn’t have to like it,” he added. Paris and Berlin are less keen The biggest obstacle to choosing a negotiator, though, might not be Putin but the EU’s two biggest capitals. France and Germany are unlikely to welcome an arrangement that gives Brussels a monopoly on representing Europe in negotiations, two European diplomats and an EU official told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made his opposition clear Thursday, calling the participation of the E3 countries in talks on Ukraine “a well-established format.” “We are also working together on this task with five representatives — from Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and Poland. I see absolutely no problem with keeping it that way,” he said. Paris also has little incentive to hand over its seat at the table. France is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and possesses Europe’s only nuclear arsenal, giving it diplomatic and military leverage that no EU institution can replicate, French MEP Fabrice Leggeri of National Rally told POLITICO, adding he could “hardly imagine” Costa or Kallas speaking for Paris. “France, Germany, and the U.K.,” the E3 countries, “will always be France, Germany and the U.K.,” Estonia’s Michal argued, adding nothing stopped them from talking bilaterally to Moscow. But on decision-making affecting the whole continent, they needed to get on board with “consensual politics.” “This is what the European Union is,” he said. “This is the basis of having this kind of consensual politics and keeping everybody together on the same page against Russia.” EU leaders are unlikely to formally appoint an envoy at Friday’s gathering, but discussions could produce a broader “understanding” about how Europe should be represented, a senior EU official said. Advertisement Advertisement Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee told POLITICO that at Friday’s talks, leaders will still need to “tease through” the issue “a little bit more.” They may not have that much time, though. Zelenskyy this week urged the EU to hurry up and pick someone — anyone — to speak for it. “I think that in November, not later, we need to accept who will represent Europe in negotiations,” he said. Giorgio Leali, Hans von der Burchard, Jacopo Barigazzi and Caroline Hug contributed to this report.
